title: Designing with Modern Transistors
intro: Short-channel transistors no longer obey the square law accurately, so nanometer design is done with simulated curves and the gm/ID methodology.

blocks.text: Why the square law is not enough

In nanometer technologies, velocity saturation, mobility degradation and DIBL change the I/V curve so much that sizing by the square law can be off by 30 percent or more. Designers therefore extract curves from simulation of the foundry model and use them to choose sizes.

Instead of Vov, use the ratio gm/ID as the design variable. In strong inversion gm/ID = 2/Vov; in weak inversion it saturates near 1/(zeta*VT), about 25 to 28 V^-1. A device with high gm/ID is efficient (lots of gm per microamp) but slow and large; one with low gm/ID is fast but power-hungry.

items: Pick gm/ID from the requirement: high gain and low noise per power favour 15 to 25; high speed favours 5 to 10.
The required gm sets ID = gm / (gm/ID).
Look up the current density ID/W at that gm/ID (it is nearly independent of W) and find W.
Read off the intrinsic gain gm*ro and the transit frequency fT from the same simulated curves for this L, to check the trade-off.

blocks.text: Typical op amp design: choose L for the needed intrinsic gain, then gm/ID for each device by its role (input pair high gm/ID for noise, mirrors lower to save area, bias devices small), compute widths, then simulate and iterate. Corners and mismatch are checked at the end.

blocks.title: gm/ID sizing
blocks.text: An input pair needs gm = 1 mS. How much current per device at gm/ID = 10 and at gm/ID = 20?
solution: ID = gm / (gm/ID). At 10: 1 mS / 10 = 100 uA. At 20: 50 uA.
Higher gm/ID halves the current but needs a considerably larger transistor, and has lower fT.
